title: Back in New York: Local 802 and the Clef Club's collapse
summary: Disgusted with Belgium, Briggs returned to New York in 1922 and found Local 802 under Con Conrad had destroyed the Black clubs' work, leaving musicians thrown out of hotels.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: When you were in Brussel's then, did you land in Paris, or did you go back to the States at that time?
I went back to the States after Ostend.
After you got in a lot of trouble there?
After Patrick's trouble.
Right.

I went back to the States because I was just disgusted. I said, I'm through with Belgium. I went back to the States and that's where I realized that it was impossible because the 802 had taken over, and the Clef, and the Amsterdam clubs went down to nothing.
Tell me about that. How did that happen? I never heard that story before. That's interesting.
Yes.
'Cause I know, you
Briggs
remember there's a guy named Whaley, who worked for Duke Ellington.
Whaley?
Whaley, he was a copiest, or something like that.
He said something to the effect, he said, "After the war, all the white guys came in, and they dried up the business for black guys."
Yeh. I can name you one of the guys. Con Conrad.
Con Conrad?
Yes. You heard of him?
Well, the name sounds vaguely familiar, but --he was the head of 802, wasn't he?
He was the head of it. You see, the thing is, there was a point where we could have worked together but he didn't want to.
Is that right? You mean you could have had mixed bands?
Briggs

Not only mixed bands. The two locals -- I mean the Clef Club and the Amsterdam Club and the 802, they could have worked together, they could have worked together, you see, but he didn't want anything.
Well, had 802 already been in existence.
Oh, yes, it had started.
But then when this guy Conrad came in, he changed the policy?
Yes, he changed the policy. He changed the policy.
I see. About when was that?
Oh, well, when I went back in '22, I'll tell you.
It was already going on then?
Yes, I'd say in three weeks.
Briggs
Well, what did he do, how did he manage this. He would go around to the club owners and say, 'I want just white bands in here?

I don't know what he did. I don't know, didn't try to find out, what he did. But the Clef Club and the Amsterdam Club had no work. They lost everything. And the colored musicians had certain jobs that they'd had, we had only two bands playing dinner music in big hotels, one of the hotels, was the Pennsylvania Hotel, now were on the street. Thrown out.
Thrown out.

That's about the time that Guy Lombardo came around. I'm not saying that they're responsible for it, but it was about that time that -- I mean what happened in New York, was -- it never happened before and one would never thing it would happen and well, the boys were thrown out on the street
Briggs

and I realized the situation, I said, to myself, I said, "Now, look, I had a job in Europe, there's no point in coming back and staying here and starting all over again, what am I going to do." I was young, I thought quick.
